newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Catholic Values uses church guidelines.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Catholic Values uses church guidelines.

text.p: The Catholic Values Investment Trust, given the green light to begin operating by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission last week, is the lastest wrinkle in "socially responsible" mutual funds.
The fund seeks companies with policies or practices reflecting values of the Roman Catholic Church.

"The (fund's) approach is to put some kind of value on core Catholic teachings. We seek companies that do not conflict with the teachings of the Catholic Church," said Walter Miller, secretary of the fund's advisory board.
"The companies may promote values abhorrent to the Church," Miller said
At present, the board won't invest in companies that
make or distribute products for birth control or abortions, in particular pharmaceutical firms. The fund's avisory board rejected a large U.S. drug company, which Miller declined to identify.
More than a dozen U.S. firms manufacture or distribute contraceptive products, according to Prudential Securities.
The fund is also considering adopting the MacBride principles on equal opportunity in Northern Ireland.
The MacBride principles promote fair-employment and anti-discrimination policies for corporations that operate in Northern Ireland.

The fund also may adopt a ban on stocks of companies that "take advantage of individuals," such as by using sweatshops and child labor. It also may take a position against companies that "promote violence in the world," Miller said.
The fund, said Miller, is not a predictable, across-the-board "socially responsible" fund. It will invest in gaming and tobacco stocks.
Would the fund invest in the Walt Disney Co, whose Miramax unit released "Priest," a controversial film that upset many Catholics when it was released 1995?
Miller said the stock did not pass its financial screens, although the movie was "an issue" for the advisory board.

After portfolio manager, Wright Investors's Services, decides on a stock, the fund's five-member board votes on whether a stock passes muster on Catholic values. It's still deciding other "Catholic screens" for a stock.

The board includes Thomas Melady, former U.S. ambassador to the Holy See; Margaret Heckler, former U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary; Thomas Monaghan, president of Domino's Pizza; Bowie Kuhn, former baseball commissioner; and William Wilson, first U.S. ambassador to the Holy See.
Miller described the fund's four main financial criteria as profitability and stability of profits; growth in earnings and capital; financial strength; and acceptance in the investment community.
The fund seeks core profit growth of at least 16.5 percent, and debt to capital ratio of no more than 30 percent.
The fund will have about 100 stocks in the portfolio, assuring no bets of more than five percent of assets in any one stock.
Top holdings include Ameritech Corp, Caterpillar Inc, Genuine Parts Co, and Pitney Bowes Inc.
Miller said the fund was seeking endorsements from the Vatican, the U.S. Conference of Bishops, and individual Catholic dioceses in the U.S.
The fund is being marketed through through broker-dealers and via a direct mail campaign through large Catholic-related institutions, such as dioceses and small churches.
Miller said the fund hopes to top $100 million in assets within a year and $350 million in three years.
